reviewer: automated review (Claude reading the cached abstracts); not a biomedical expert review
method: Each verbatim quote was read in the context of its full cached abstract (data/raw/pubmed/abstracts). Dominant-negative claims against a curated loss-of-function mechanism were kept when they describe patient variants, but flagged in the condition caveat as a refinement of loss of function rather than an opposite direction.

ev:pubmed:37537625:claim:0.reason: Single-patient (n-of-1) intrathecal magnesium trial designed around the electrophysiology of a gain-of-function GRIN1 mutation in the patient; the quote is a treatment description but states the patient variant is gain of function.

ev:pubmed:29365063:claim:0.reason: De novo GRIN1 missense mutations in polymicrogyria patients increased agonist potency or reduced proton inhibition (gain of function); the abstract notes previous GRIN1 mutations generally caused loss of function, so both directions occur in different patients.

cond:G2P00033.note: Published patient series describe both gain- and loss-of-function SCN2A variants; gain of function is typical of neonatal-onset epilepsy and loss of function of later-onset epilepsy, autism and intellectual disability, so which applies depends on the individual variant.

cond:G2P00222.note: One early report predicted (but did not prove) that a truncated SATB2 protein might act dominant-negatively; the curated loss-of-function mechanism is not seriously challenged by a single predicted case.

cond:G2P00251.note: Most SCN1A epilepsy variants (including Dravet syndrome) cause loss of function, but a distinct group of gain-of-function SCN1A variants causes familial hemiplegic migraine and an early-onset non-Dravet epilepsy that may respond differently to medication; the direction depends on the variant.

cond:G2P00366.note: The two papers describe KCNA2 variants that cause loss of channel function with an added dominant-negative effect on the normal channel; this is a refinement of loss of function, not an opposite direction (gain-of-function KCNA2 variants are curated as a separate condition).
cond:G2P00366.caveat: Both kept claims describe dominant-negative LOSS of function, so they refine rather than oppose the curated loss-of-function mechanism; a curator may prefer not to label this condition as having both directions.

cond:G2P00467.note: Gene2Phenotype lists gain of function, but the discovery and follow-up papers for the recurrent progressive myoclonus epilepsy variant p.Arg320His report dominant-negative loss of function, and most other KCNC1 variants are also loss of function; this disagreement needs expert review.
cond:G2P00467.caveat: The same recurrent variant (p.Arg320His) that the curated entry calls gain of function is reported as dominant-negative loss of function in three papers; this may be a curation error rather than a scientific dispute and should be checked by a curator.

cond:G2P00546.note: In-frame SPTAN1 variants acting dominant-negatively cause the epilepsy/neurodevelopmental condition, while truncating loss-of-function variants cause milder distal muscle weakness, motor neuropathy or ataxia; the two variant classes give different conditions.
cond:G2P00546.caveat: PMIDs 39371122 and 40023774 appear to be the preprint and published versions of the same 14-family study, so the independent evidence is three studies, not four; the loss-of-function phenotypes (distal myopathy, motor neuropathy, ataxia) differ from the curated epilepsy condition.

cond:G2P00548.note: Published cases describe both loss-of-function GNAO1 variants (mainly epileptic encephalopathy) and gain-of-function variants (mainly movement disorders) in patients; which applies depends on the individual variant.
cond:G2P00548.caveat: Two of the kept claims are dominant-negative (compatible with loss of function); the opposing gain-of-function evidence comes from PMIDs 29758257 and 28747448 and concerns movement-disorder patients rather than epileptic encephalopathy.

cond:G2P00566.note: Published cases describe both loss-of-function GRIN2A variants (null variants and some missense, milder phenotypes) and gain-of-function missense variants in the channel region (more severe phenotypes); which applies depends on the individual variant.
cond:G2P00566.caveat: The gain-of-function evidence rests mainly on PMID 30544257; the other two gain claims are passing statements in reviews, and the dominant-negative claim refines loss of function for a single variant.

cond:G2P00586.note: Published cases describe both loss-of-function GRIN2B variants and gain-of-function pore-region variants (for example in West syndrome) in patients; which applies depends on the individual variant.

cond:G2P00594.note: Neither flagged paper concerns WWOX patient variants in the developmental disorder (one is a cancer review, one a speculative fusion gene), so the curated loss-of-function mechanism stands uncontested.

cond:G2P00636.note: The only flagged paper speculates that some NRXN1 variants might act as gain of function; no patient evidence for that, so loss of function stands.

cond:G2P00789.note: The one flagged paper concerns KCNQ2 variants causing peripheral nerve hyperexcitability (not neonatal epilepsy) acting dominant-negatively, which is still a form of loss of function.

cond:G2P00800.note: A single paper reports gain-of-function GABRA1 variants at one specific position (P260) in children with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, a different presentation from juvenile myoclonic epilepsy; loss of function remains the mechanism for the curated condition.

cond:G2P01018.note: The flagged paper is a mouse overexpression study; it does not show gain-of-function FOXG1 variants in patients.

cond:G2P01021.note: One in-vitro study tentatively suggests that ADNP variants in the nuclear localisation signal might have a gain-of-function component, while most variants behave as loss of function; this is a single tentative finding.

cond:G2P01031.note: The flagged paper is a zebrafish knockdown study and does not concern patient variants; gain of function stands.

cond:G2P01058.note: Angelman syndrome is caused by loss of maternal UBE3A, while extra copies or hyperactivating UBE3A variants are linked to a different autism-related presentation; both directions exist but cause different conditions.

cond:G2P01128.note: One paper reports two siblings with a homozygous STXBP1 variant showing increased synaptic transmission (gain of function); the usual heterozygous STXBP1 variants act by loss of function.

cond:G2P01160.note: The flagged papers concern DYRK1A overexpression in Down syndrome, leukaemia or Alzheimer research, not DYRK1A variants in patients with this disorder; loss of function stands.

cond:G2P01456.note: Most KCNQ2 epileptic encephalopathy variants act by dominant-negative loss of function, while a smaller group of gain-of-function variants also causes encephalopathy; which applies depends on the individual variant.
cond:G2P01456.caveat: The curated gain-of-function mechanism likely refers to a minority of KCNQ2 DEE variants; the literature here says most DEE variants are dominant-negative loss of function.

cond:G2P01473.note: Most GABRG2 epilepsy variants reduce receptor function (some with a dominant-negative effect), but a few missense variants increase function and are linked to severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy; the direction depends on the variant.
cond:G2P01473.caveat: Three kept claims are dominant-negative (a loss-of-function subtype); the genuine opposite direction (gain of function) comes from PMIDs 39642202 and 40570274.

cond:G2P01600.note: Gene2Phenotype lists gain of function, but a 2020 series of 14 patients argues the de novo missense EEF1A2 variants act through loss of function (haploinsufficiency), while a mouse model suggests a toxic or dominant-negative effect; the mechanism is genuinely unsettled.

cond:G2P01608.note: Gene2Phenotype lists dominant negative, but large patient series describe SCN8A epileptic encephalopathy variants as gain of function (often responsive to sodium-channel blockers) and a separate group of loss-of-function variants causing milder generalized epilepsy or intellectual disability; the curated label should be checked.
cond:G2P01608.caveat: The curated "dominant negative" label is itself unusual: the large patient series and reviews read here describe DEE variants as gain of function; a curator should check the source of the curated mechanism.
